utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Registrar, would you have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, let me be sure that the interpreters can hear me. Good morning to all the interpreters, and I would also like to say good morning to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and Mr. Nice, Mr. Tochilovsky. And good morning to Defence counsel, Mr. Greaves, Mr. Londrovic, and to the accused. I believe that we can now begin, because the witness, who couldn't testify a few days ago because he was sick, I think can now be brought in. Is that correct? Mr. Greaves? Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am only on my feet to explain that the gentleman sitting on my right, if this is acceptable to the Court, is Dr. Duits, the psychiatrist who has prepared a report and who I would be calling, I forecast, with your leave immediately after the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask Mr. Greaves, who is going to call in Mr. van den Bussche -- is he feeling better? Mr. Greaves, is he feeling better today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I haven't actually spoken to him, but I anticipate so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope he is the one who can talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any problem in having Dr. Duits sitting here?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is a procedure with which I am entirely familiar in my own system, and I have no objection to my learned friend having the assistance of Dr. Duits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges see Dr. Duits' presence as an advantage. All right. We can now move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If we may have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, doctor. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do. We hope that you will be able to speak today. Do you feel better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel a little bit better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not really great?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we say in France, the shoemakers are the ones who have the worst shoes. Well, you are a doctor, and perhaps you didn't take proper care of yourself. Well, we'll try to continue with our work. First of all I am going to ask you to take an oath. You took an oath. All right. You don't have to do that, then. Thank you, Judge Rodrigues, for reminding me of that. You may be seated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. van den Bussche, I will be as quick as I can, in view of your condition. Can you first of all help us about this. Your full name is Bernard van den Bussche, and you are a forensic psychiatrist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you initially sworn in 1985 as a permanent judicial expert by the Court in Amsterdam?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind, please, as to tell their honours what your professional qualifications are?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1985 I worked for the Forensic Psychiatric Service, Amsterdam, as a forensic psychiatrist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speak slowly. Speak slowly. Don't try to fatigue your voice too quickly. Just answer gently, quietly, and also allow the interpreters to do a proper job in interpreting you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Forensic Psychiatric Service in the Netherlands, all branches of the Dutch Ministry of Justice. And the Forensic Psychiatric Service, Amsterdam is one of the biggest, most qualified and experienced compared with the others. Therefore, we were asked by the Dutch Ministry of Justice to cooperate with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you practiced as a forensic psychiatrist, Mr. van den Bussche?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whereabouts did you qualify as a forensic psychiatrist? Was that at university or medical school?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: University.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which university did you attend?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The University of Utrecht.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from your qualification as a doctor and a forensic psychiatrist, do you have any other medical qualifications?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of your duties as a permanent judicial expert with the court, are you regularly involved in making reports for the courts of the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the court in Amsterdam and the higher court I made in about 15 years about 400 psychiatric reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you were about to finish. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: And besides that, I do risk assessment reports on behalf of the Dutch Ministry of Justice in special clinics where serial killers or serial rapists are compulsory treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is what you are saying that serial killers and serial rapists is, in effect, your speciality?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you made that your specialty throughout your period of service with the Dutch Justice Ministry?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Dutch ministry asked me to do those risk assessments -- risk assessment reports because of my experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, help us about this, please. Did you, during the course of your duties, then go to see the defendant, Goran Jelisic, earlier this month?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, as a result of that, prepare a report?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dated the 8th of November 1999?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I think that's the report which has been filed with the Tribunal, and I hope that you have it. And you can answer any questions from the Prosecution concerning your report.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. van den Bussche, would you be so kind to wait there, please, and to answer such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice represents The Office of the Prosecutor and he will ask some questions. Mr. Nice, please proceed now. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, in order to save your voice, I will try and ask questions, sometimes compendious questions which may be capable of the yes, no answer, leaving your voice freer for those occasions when you will need to expand. So the questioning, if it works, will be a little unusual, but will be aimed at helping you. First, it's correct, isn't it, that although you had access to the earlier psychiatric and psychological reports on this man, you have not seen a record of his interviews, and you know nothing of the evidence that has been given by witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And that's a pity. It's not an usual situation in the Netherlands. The psychiatric interview is only a small part of the complete psychiatric examination. And usually I have to read for about four 'til ten hours all the trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, do feel free to add if you want to, but you've given the answer. The second point is that on this occasion you interviewed the man alone, but for an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again the compendious question is this: With psychiatric examinations you always have to be careful about the subject being dishonest and attempting to mislead or to manipulate the psychiatrist, and it is therefore preferable, when possible, to have two people present at the examination, and not one? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man is a man who is shown to be both dishonest and manipulative; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that you, therefore, suffered the disadvantage, and there's no criticism in anything I say, but you suffered the disadvantage of not having a second expert at your shoulder or by your side to check on what he may have been trying to achieve; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree completely with you. In the Dutch court system it is even a fault if you speak with a severe criminal alone. So I always advise my colleagues to talk with two persons, and then you can choose between two of a kind or two of a different kind. I prefer to talk with a psychiatrist and a psychologist because some of them even can cheat two psychiatrists, and a psychologist, you can better rely on a psychologist because he can do more objective tests to find out the manipulation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the interests, again, of saving your voice and dealing with things in an orderly way, it may be helpful if I ask you to open your report at, I think, page 5, and I will try and deal with the particular questions I have in relation to your report in sequence. Then I'll turn to a few other questions about other reports and a few other general propositions that I'd like you to help us with. Again, many of these questions may be capable of being dealt with briefly. Of course, at the end of it, if there's something you want to add and feel I haven't explored, you will be allowed to do so without any hesitation, I'm sure. On page 5, he tells you, under case history, that his former attorneys, and he names them, wanted him to commit suicide and were contemptible, that they advised him to keep silent and offered him money, and that his family was threatened. He didn't, of course, point to any proof of this. Did he provide any detail beyond what's set out here?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down, we see that he identifies the offenders who he said were at liberty and goes on to give an account of forming liaisons in prison with Croats and, indeed, with Muslims. Ingratiation is making himself popular with the very group of people who had been his victims consistent with his being both manipulative and narcissistic?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found him more childish and immature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Three lines up from the bottom of this page, he told you no more than that he had acted under duress, that he shot 15 people, but then he said he saved hundreds. He provided you no detail of the alleged hundreds that he saved.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I couldn't check it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He, of course, then went on to say that he was being made a national scapegoat. Setting himself in the big picture is consistent with the narcissism and/or the childishness.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Over the page, please, to page 6, as you summarise it, just under halfway down, he says: "'I was forced to kill, by my superiors. They gave me the name Adolf. If I hadn't followed the orders of those monsters, I would have been killed.'" You may have other notes, I don't know, but did he give you any more detail of how he was forced to kill than that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that some friends of his were shot in front of Muslims when they denied to follow the orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you check whether that was a version he had ever given before or whether this was a completely new version of events, being forced to see others being shot for disobedience?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read it in the other reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm going to come to just a couple aspects of the other reports and the way his stories change. But since I want to deal with this report in an orderly way, you would accept, would you not, that if this version is new and different and if one can see in the earlier reports a developing series of different stories, then the different stories obviously undermine his reliability, don't they?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a possibility, but he has also other attorneys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He blames the other attorneys at some stage --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- for forcing him to give different stories, but I'll come to that. If we put that on one side, and if somebody gives, first, one account, then a stronger account, then a different account, and, in your report, yet another different account, that obviously goes to show he may just simply be being dishonest.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, just a little further down the same paragraph, he says: "'On one occasion, I fell to my knees and begged to not have to go on any more. I was informed that I shouldn't think, but simply carry out orders.'" I don't know if you have any more detail of the falling to his knees, but the question again I want to ask you is this: Did you find any earlier reference to this form of pleading by him?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any more detail of what he said happened on this occasion, beyond what you've set out here?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of page 6, you set out the following, about ten lines up: "When the discussion focused on his upcoming 7 to 8 days of defence, tears appeared in his eyes, and the defendant started to cry ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I hope I'm not going too fast for the interpreters and that they've got copies. I'll slow down a little. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "'I hate the idea of seeing and hearing all those people --'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nice. I'm waiting for the French version. It takes a little longer to say it in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was fine up to this point. There it is. I see where you are. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "'I hate the idea of seeing and hearing all those people who both on request, and also spontaneously are coming to bear witness ...'" and then that paragraph continues. If we go on about another eight or nine lines, you set out this: "Following deeper questioning, it emerged that over the last few months, the defendant has regularly been crying, when alone." Now, my question is this: The first tears relate to his defence witnesses; the second tears, were those also for himself and for his defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was crying all the time at that moment, for about four or five minutes, and I really had to relax him, to get himself in a better condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were the tears for himself?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the tears were not for himself, but in my opinion, he was confused between feelings of intimacy to others and feelings of aggression and all kinds of different mixed feelings, and he didn't know until now how to manage them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You, I think, will be able to confirm from the material you've read that there is no reference, I think, anywhere else in the material to his showing spontaneous remorse, tearful or otherwise, for his victims.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the first occasion of crying is crying which we saw related to his emotion at people coming to give evidence for him; it's not tears about his victims.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the English version, I'm getting to the end of this passage which comes on page 7, and in the French version, it must be at the foot of page 11, I think. Yes. Two things really. He says that he was arrested and tortured -- I beg your pardon. He says that the account that he was arrested and tortured by the Croat army was untrue, that he'd been under pressure from his former attorneys to make those claims. I'm a little confused as to what page 9, paragraph 2 means in the report of Dr. Duits and Dr. van der Veen, but without doing a paper chase, can you confirm that what he was instructing you to say should be rubbed out completely was the account of torture in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that by the time of his first psychiatric examination, he was already being represented by the attorney who he says he trusted, even if one of the other attorneys was still involved in his case at that time?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he says he made these allegations in response to his attorneys, but one of his trusted attorneys was also already on his team.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Londrovic. But -- yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we go on now to page 9 in the English, page 12, halfway down page 12 in the French, he says this: "Nonetheless, the defendant wished to state that the previous report writers, Dr. Duits and van der Veen had written down things which he had not said. Once the undersigned had asked why he had not corrected the reports, since he had taped the entire previous examination interviews, there was a moment of silence and the ice appeared to have been broken." What was it, according to Jelisic, that Dr. Duits and Dr. van der Veen had written down either incorrect or untruthfully.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him, but he didn't tell me. I asked him, I said, "You taped everything." And then he said to me nothing any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So either he was being dishonest with you or he was being untruthful or dishonest with them? It has to follow, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn over, please, to page 10 in the English, where in the middle of the page you make the point, and I think you've made it already, that he emphasised his position as a victim in all of this, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but, in my opinion, a little bit less than in the previous reports. But just a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, he had obviously had the advantage of reading the previous reports, because he commented on them, and he was thus in a position to act and to change his behaviour to accord with what would be wanted of him?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a possibility that he is manipulating, but, on the other hand, I made the report one year later, so a person can change in a year. That's also a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a person, of course, who is found to have been theatrical in nature in any event, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a theatrical person is both more likely to and more able to mislead people such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's why it was such a pity that we couldn't test him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same page in the English, a few paragraphs down, three quarters of the way down the page you say this: "In parallel to these considerations, during his examination the defendant started to show more true remorse and feelings of guilt in respect of his victims and their family members." Do I take it that you are saying that this first demonstration of remorse, of which you are aware, happened in your very examination?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because there is no evidence of it happening earlier, is there?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On reflection, and I will probably remember to ask you this question again at the end, but on reflection, this has to be possible, doesn't it; that he was simply doing this because he knew he was the subject of criticism for showing no remorse in earlier reports?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 11 you make this point, and it's in the first complete paragraph. I'll see if I can find the French. Yes, I think it's at the foot of page 14, if that assists, Your Honour. You deal with his having narcissistic traits based on a primarily negative self-image. You then go on to say: "He maintained surface object relationships, was fundamentally uncertain and easily influenced. Unconsciously he was searching for a father identification figure. He tends too easily to identify with people in a power position. For them he can offer little resistance and is easily influenced." Now, the characteristic of being easily influenced by people in power is not something that will be immediately apparent, is it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you see him, not. But he looks around 30 years old, but in his emotional life I think he is about 17, 18 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But the point is that these aspects of the potential to be influenced are something that you are either going to discover at a psychiatric examination or you are going to have to discover by some prolonged contact with the man?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the psychiatric interview and his life history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we can go to the next -- well, you do say in the same section, I needn't take you to the passage, you say in the same section that he has had suicidal ideas. This is entirely based on his own account, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can go to the next section headed Diagnostic Observations. You set out at the beginning of Diagnostic Observations, page 13 and 17 in the French, that he has admitted having killed 15 people under duress. Various conclusions in your report follow. If, in fact, he was not acting under duress, may I take it that many, most, or it may be all of your conclusions fall and come to nothing?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which conclusions do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, conclusions about remorse, in particular the conclusions about remorse we are going to come to later on. But do those conclusions fall away? Must we disregard them, if he was not, in fact, acting under duress?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If it's not true, what he is telling me, then he must have behaved during the crimes in a different way than he is telling me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I am not criticising you at all, because you had limited material to go on. I just want to understand your report. So that from this moment on you are working on the basis that what he tells you is correct --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only base I have is what he is telling me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's the limitation of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. And you accept that on findings of facts, it's the Judges who have to decide whether and to what extent he was acting under any duress?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the foot of page 13, which will be either the foot of 17 or over to 18 in the French, you make some observations about wars. I pick it up at the foot of 13 where you say that wartime conditions influence personality; that no two wars are the same; that parties to war, in your opinion, behave as if with antisocial, psychopathic borderliners, hiding behind and basing their actions on rational and national motives. Without being critical, doctor, it's fair to say that this is outside your area of special expertise?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, in a certain way. What I wanted to make clear was on page --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to go on to the next page, so if you want me to read the next bit, I will as well. Shall we go through that and then it will save your voice if I ask the question again. Over at page 14 you say that all parties were active in splitting manipulation and paranoid projection. You say psychiatric primitive defences are characteristic for borderline personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you then say this: In a climate of this kind it is adaptive, understandable, and easy or easily empathised with and, given the circumstances, relatively healthy for an individual to develop such personality characteristics with a view to survival. I'll just complete it, then I'll give your voice its free rein. Some individuals are able to handle the situation and do so within normal social standards. Others, often the minority, fail. And if they have an imperfect identity and are sensitive to identification with, for example, an aggressive leader. You then say there are notable psychopaths, who are already psychopaths prior to the war and come into a playground, as it were, to live out their sadistic lust. Now, if I tell you the questions I want to ask, and then you can give a single answer. First, your analysis of warring parties having leaders manifesting antisocial, psychopathic borderline characteristics, and projecting those onto others, is outside your area of expertise and, unless I've missed something or unless we've missed something, not supported by research or learned material. And the second question is: Are you really suggesting that a majority or a substantial minority of people will identify in this way, and that it would be relatively healthy for people to do so?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to make clear is this. In Holland we have much expertise with the victims of concentration camps, and there are some two or three special clinics in Holland where, 'til now, still victims are treated. And strange enough, you see that quite often the survivors, the only survivors of those concentration camps have a borderline personality because the only way they could survive was by also lying, with a little bit of cheating, and not be honest. So if you see somebody with a borderline personality, after a war, it can mean two things. It can mean he was already a borderline before the war and already before the war emotionally disturbed, but it can also be a kind of adaptive mechanism to survive the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, and am grateful for your explanation. I understand that in relation to those who are true victims. But Jelisic, who now denies even being tortured in Croatia or Serbia, is in no sense a true victim. He is a perpetrator. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, whatever learning there may be in Holland about the ability to survive of the victims doesn't really bear on this issue at all, does it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is no -- 'til now, there is no psychiatrist who did research on war offenders, and that that's the point, I have no reference material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then finally on your report, and then I'll just turn to the other questions I have, you make the point right at the end of the report that German perpetrators of war crimes lived for years in South America as diligent family men. Again, there is no learning on this, this question number one. And question number 2 is, even if you are right, that war crime perpetrators lived as diligent family men in South America, they had a real interest in keeping their behaviour good and their profile low, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Dealing with the only points that I would need to make on the other three reports, and to some degree I've covered them already, you are aware of the fact that in the first report to Dr. Elsmann he gave an account of being tortured in Croatia and expressing in fairly, I think, straightforward terms that he was put under pressure to kill on the basis that he would be killed otherwise. Do you remember that in the most general terms?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That can be found, if the Court finds page references helpful, at page 3 of that report. I don't go into it in detail. The point I am going to make is a short one. In the report of Dr. Herfst in April at page 3 he gives a detailed account again of his escape and of his being tortured. On this occasion he speaks of a hand grenade around his neck, of being wounded with a knife, and of having red hot cinders on his feet. So that the account is enlarged. On page 4 of the report he sets out how the army commander called him Adolf and said he had to kill, and gave him a list: That he had no choice, and otherwise, if he didn't obey, he would be killed. He was provided with alcohol and pills. In the next report of Dr. Duits we see at page 10 -- well, 9 and 10, we see the account of torture continued, with an account at the top of the page of cutting veins on the back of his feet and putting hot coals on them. But at the foot of page 10 we see this: At the police station they threatened him with the words, "This bullet is worth more than your head, if you don't do what you are told. You must obey and ask no questions." He was also threatened that his sister would be raped if he didn't do the job properly. He then had to take a group of people to the station and murder them. We know, from your report, that he has abandoned all suggestion that he was tortured and has produced to you a new and different version of the pressure that was put on him to make him kill. The development and the changes of these accounts show, do they not, that as a historian he is simply not to be relied upon. You would accept that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a person who manipulates, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as between these different accounts over time, it's impossible to choose between them, or to say any one of them is preferable to the other?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What it is possible to say is that the way he develops his account, in knowledge of what has gone before, shows that he is responding in a manipulative way to what the psychiatrists have found out about him?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but also it's a very childish way of manipulation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you can look immediately through it, like you do now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you haven't heard the evidence and, I repeat, absolutely no criticism in that, but can I just summarise for you a few things that have been given in evidence and may or may not be accepted by the Trial Chamber. The evidence shows that he was enthusiastic to kill; that he killed people on his own account, without any reference to authority; that he swore at victims; that he beat victims; that even after he was stopped from killing by a superior officer, he returned, expressing desires to kill. He even admits returning to look at the prisoners after he had been stopped from killing. He also brags of the numbers he had killed, with such expressions as, "I've done seven today so far and I'll do another eight." Or claiming to have killed either 76 or 86 people, claiming up to 150 killings. And speaking of, "Well, that will be 68 balijas," which is a derogatory word for Muslims, "less." If he did those things without the evidence of anybody standing behind him making him do and say those things, then that completely contradicts the account he gave to you of acting under duress.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next thing is this: A preeminent characteristic of the personality disorder that you and all the experts found is manipulation and control; would you accept that? A desire to control events rather than to be --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not completely. In fact, we are saying in all the reports the same thing. We give it another name, the personality disorder, but personality disorders are what we call clustered. So this personality disorder, anti-personality disorder, and borderline personality disorder belong to cluster B, and cluster B, all those personality disorders in cluster B, they have no overlap. So if you see a person with traces of two of those personality disorders, then that's why I choose the name of personality disorder, not otherwise specified, which are the traits of both of those personality disorders. The crucial thing in the personality disorder is instability, instability in feelings, instability in self-judgement, instability in judging others, impulsiveness, et cetera, and not so much the will to control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But there is within him, and it may be that you and Dr. Duits will not necessarily agree on this, but there is within him manifestation of a desire to control as manifested by manipulation.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he has some anti-social traits and he wants to be in power, if you mean that by "control".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also true, and this relates to the issue of danger that you address in your report, it's true, isn't it, that -- the following two propositions are true: Proposition 1: The desire to control is either "the" or "a" principle characteristic of the true psychopath; proposition 2, which is separate from that proposition but linked to it, proposition 2 is that the learning shows that once someone has killed once, his resistance to killing again is substantially reduced, he finds it easier to kill having done it once.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second is right, that's correct. The first one is not completely correct. You have to add that a psychopath doesn't feel sorry for what he's done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, because his sole interest is in control. He starts off controlling people in one way or another; he finds the measure of control unsatisfying; he moves to greater control, typically tying someone up or imprisoning them; his ultimate step has to be to kill them.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's almost, for a psychopath, a sexual lust.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So that in this case, it is in truth, at best, impossible to say anything about how dangerous this man is, but there are indicators in his personality and in his history of killing that he will remain a danger.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that question already in my report. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I should have asked you this: You know in his account -- perhaps you don't know, but in his accounts he said he was incapable of looking at his victims when he shot them. If there were clear evidence, and there is from the photographs, that he looks absolutely at his victim as he shoots him, that again would tend to undermine what he says to you about being under duress, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a form of manipulation, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I come back, I think, to my last proposition, and I'm grateful to you for having had the voice to answer my questions so far. If we set on one side his account of how he came to kill, because it's so varied and he's shown to be dishonest, if we acknowledge that his vulnerability to authority figures wouldn't be manifest on him, not something you wear like a badge, it's got to be discovered, then the problem that may face the Chamber is how he came to kill at all. You're not suggesting in your report that anyone or a large number of people would behave in this way, that is, go out and kill people; you're not suggesting that's a majority human trait?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Accordingly, it comes to this, doesn't it, that the easiest way of finding out if somebody is prepared to kill would be to ask them.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, it's strange, what happened, if he's telling the truth about his life history. Usually, when you are a psychopath and when you start to kill people, you have already aggression regulation problems in your youth, and I could not find any of them. So what you have to do, you have to interview his parents, his schoolmaster, to find out if the things he's telling me about his life history or his youth is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But given that you wouldn't know that this man was likely to do what he eventually did, he's the sort of personality, is this not right, who, were he asked to do this sort of thing by authority figures --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- recognising that he would be given power and status if he responded to the request, he's the sort of person who might fall to be a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my opinion, he has almost no identity of his own. So that means that if a bad guy passed by in power, he becomes a bad guy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were a couple of other questions; I'll just deal with them very briefly. If a person is in remorse for what he or she has done, is he or she likely to be compelled in the brain to relive what has happened, to rerun that awful history?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a difficult question to answer, because we are talking about facts that happened six, seven years ago, and in every mind, if I look to myself and I think about facts that happened six or seven years ago, there are always distortions in the memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I quite understand that, but if somebody he's killed not by mistake but as a result of a crisis not of his making, and he is genuinely in remorse of that, is he likely to relive that experience?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a person who turns the corner and faces the reality of what he's done is likely to relive, to whatever degree possible, the awful events that have happened.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this man was always cautious, wasn't he, with you and with the psychiatrists who examined him before you, to limit the number of people he killed.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the number?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware -- I think you weren't aware -- that in his interview he speaks of up to 20, and, indeed, he speaks of 20 on occasions.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was talking to me about 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be difficult, wouldn't it, if you were genuinely remorseful and being honest with the psychiatrist not to have a reasonably accurate knowledge of the number of people you'd killed.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His very inaccuracy, changing between 15 and 20, may be another indicator that he simply isn't being honest.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Greaves. Re-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. van den Bussche, can I ask you this, please: You've told Their Honours that, yes, he is capable of manipulation but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Greaves. I haven't heard your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told Their Honours that the defendant is capable of trying to manipulate during the course of the interview with you, but you also described it as a childish means of manipulation. May we conclude from this that you were able, at all times during your dealings with the defendant, to see through those attempts at manipulation.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I've quite a lot of experience in that field. I have even interviewed people where I didn't feel safe at all in the same room, and I had the feeling that I would be lucky if I could leave the room. So this interview was, for me, quite relaxed, and in my opinion, the worst psychopaths are the smart ones and clever ones, and he was manipulating in a childish way, immature way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we conclude that the conclusions to which you have come in your report and the evidence which you've given today has taken due account of his ability to manipulate.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In coming to the conclusions that you do in your report and the evidence about him which you have given today, have you, as it were, come to those conclusions after giving due account to the attempts at manipulation that he has made with you?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way he manipulates is easy to see and not a smart way, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just take it a little further, when you conclude something about it, you conclude it after giving allowance for that manipulation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. At some stage in your report, you refer to him or use the phrase "true remorse." Perhaps I can just refresh your memory as to the page. I'm sorry. I've lost it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's page 10, if that will help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry. I can't find my own note.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 10 of the English version of your report, Dr. van den Bussche, you refer to him as having -- or an expression of "true remorse." Again, was that something you were able to conclude about him, having, as it were, factored in the degree of manipulation that he was capable of?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those feelings were real at the moment. His emotional life is not really mature but those feelings he was showing at that moment were not feelings of manipulation, in my eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been asked about this by my learned friend, in general terms, about people who have killed before. It is undoubtedly right that this defendant has killed. Did you see in him any particular aspect which gave you cause for concern that this individual would be likely to repeat the experience?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't conclude that. For that you would have to do comprehensive psychological tests. Because in an interview with me, he is not showing any feelings of lust or he is not saying that he likes to kill. Maybe he is manipulating in that, I don't know, but then you have to find out by comprehensive tests or psychological tests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the remark in general about people who have killed before cannot, one way or the other, be imputed to this defendant without further tests.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everybody is different and it's not good to generalise too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking, please, at page 8 of the English version of your report, Mr. van den Bussche. You were asked a question about the defendant saying the torture that he had experienced in Croatia and Serbia, that he was now withdrawing that. Did he mention anything at all about Serbia when he was talking to you?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the only reference he made was to torture taking place in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said to me he had to skip the torture in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. van den Bussche, sir, I want to ask you this, please. You had put to you a series of pieces of evidence picked out by my learned friend from the Prosecution's case. Can I ask you this, please. We've heard evidence in this case of the defendant, firstly, being friendly towards the Muslim community prior to the war; of him giving assistance, at personal risk, to Muslims during the war and during the relevant time when he was killing people; and thirdly, of him giving assistance, again at personal risk, after the war to Muslims. Can you say anything about how that profile fits with the picture of someone going off and enthusiastically and joyfully killing Muslims at about the same time?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two pictures don't match with each other, in my opinion

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you wait there, please, and answer further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to consult with my colleagues about what we are going to do next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to take a 20-minute break and ask you to remain available to the Tribunal. And this may give you some time to drink some hot tea in order to answer the Judge's questions. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can resume now. And we will move to the Judges questions for Mr. van den Bussche. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. van den Bussche. Good morning, Mr. van den Bussche. We were very interested in listening to you, and I am sorry not to be a psychiatrist. I think this is the greatest mission, to know the human -- to go deep into the human soul, perhaps. I just gathered two things, mainly, being a layman, from your testimony, from the reports, especially from -- to start with, from your testimony you said that our accused, Jelisic, his emotional life is -- could be 17 or 18 years. Now, what could this imply? First, would that mean that he hasn't got the full discernment of his actions? Would that mean his discernment is lacking? You don't need -- just tell me "yes" or "no," the way you did, if your voice is not good.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I will try to explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, he doesn't know the dimension of his actions? Is that what you are implying?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not completely. A personality disorder is an emotional development disorder. It's always an emotional development disorder. And it doesn't mean that a person doesn't have the capacity of his free will. He still can have -- he still can have the capacity of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- and discernment. So he knows the dimension of his actions?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would that also imply that although he knows the dimension, he lacks the control of a mature person? He can't control himself?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a certain way, yes. To a certain degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He would feel an unresistible urge to do things?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And as far as his relationship with people, which you mentioned people have got over higher authority. Would that mean that he would be easily led by them?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Very easily. Why, because his emotional life is 17 or 18?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only his emotional life, but also his identity is like somebody from 17, 18 years old. He is, in fact, still an adolescent and not a mature adult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps the age you mentioned, 17 or 18, they have got a strong personality, they have an opinion of their own, they even are sometimes stubborn?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, I have difficulty understanding that. At that age you are easily led. Is it --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They are easily led?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you have discernment --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: More easily influenced by people in authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you know what you are doing, discernment is full?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You don't question that as a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Full discernment?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in your diagnosis too you mentioned the characteristics. One of them is the dysthymic. What is the meaning of dysthymic?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a mild, mild form of depression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'll talk slowly. I got here -- yes, you would like -- dysthymic?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very mild form of depression. Slightly depressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would that lead to the actions that he is accused of?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is related to the circumstances he is in at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: At the moment of the --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the detention, that he had to go to his trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That he is here, you mean?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But not when he was killing?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It does not affect the killing --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, at that time he wasn't -- he wasn't dysthymic. I am talking in my report about the situation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: At this moment. But in your report when you say -- in your testimony, that he has got a negative self-image, narcissistic antisocial behaviour; this was not now, this was also before?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personality disorder is also -- is already before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It's continuous and a desire to control?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: But dysthymic is at this moment only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But others are part of his personality?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, this premise could also make it more or less possible to commit such crimes, if you have got this diagnosis, a person of this character?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Is likely to commit such crimes?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not likely. Some persons with this personality disorder commit these crimes, but maybe not more than with other personality disorders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not more?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except when the antisocial component is very high. But if you look to borderline personality disorder, I think the percentage of total population is a little bit less than one per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from borderline personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are speaking of the Dutch population or the world population?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The world population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: World population?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So this one per cent we can expect them to do such things?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's -- you can't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We would be in real danger.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But still, suppose -- I mean, we know that they are more likely, if I understood rightly, that they would be -- they would commit aggression and so on. But they still have the discernment; they know what they are doing completely?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That does not interfere with the discernment?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: They know what they are doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They know what they are doing?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, doctor. As you were answering Mr. Nice's questions, I noted down my own. I did that taking into account the assertions -- with the realisation that assertions of that type always have to be somewhat moderated. And I am trying to set up some kind of a structure for an analysis. We have our own ways of looking at reality, of course, and I've used my own. If we take the relationship between authority and obedience, as concerns Mr. Jelisic, how would you say that those two extremes, the two extremes of that relationship, how would they operate; that is, the extremes of authority and obedience?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he will be obedient to people of a higher authority and of an older age because he is looking or searching for a kind of father identification. So he will be, I think, less obedient to people of his same age, and I think he shows more resistance too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we go beyond discretion, which I think is a key question for understanding Mr. Jelisic's personality, if we go beyond issue of identification, one would be able to say that if he had not completed his process of identification, he would not feel equal in a relationship that he might have. Could we conclude that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can conclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, he isn't capable of having an adult relationship because he had not yet constructed a relationship of authority.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had, in fact, no good relations with his father, and that is, in fact, one of his biggest problems afterwards in his whole life, and he is still looking for a father figure. When such a figure passes by, he is easily influenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but I've got to wait to hear the interpretation. We are used to some breaks which can get in the way of our discussion. If I look at a different relationship, the relationship between utility and lies, is there a close relationship between those parameters, or does one thing have nothing to do with the other?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get the question completely. The relation between lies and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Utility, from the point of view of moral judgement. Perhaps you're familiar with Colbert's work, who raises that question to some extent, the process of moral reasoning, starting from a heteroautonomous relationship to an autonomous relationship. I think that one could make the relationship between lies and utility, because we saw that Mr. Jelisic lied on several occasions. Could we say that lying has something to do with some idea of utility or usefulness from the point of view of moral judgement?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic has a lack or a not complete conscience, and he is, in fact, also in the development of his conscience, still a child who wants to avoid punishment; therefore, he doesn't have a real inner conscience, but if he sees that something is wrong and he's going to be punished, he doesn't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question that I have. I think I'm following the order that I picked up from your answers to Mr. Nice's questions. I'm thinking about another relationship, and that is the one of autonomy and dependence. I believe that the fact that Mr. Jelisic had not really structured or completed his own identity could create a certain degree of dependency, specifically in relation to some authority figures. How do you see this relationship, that is, between autonomy and dependence, as far as Mr. Jelisic goes?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic suffers from what we call invaluation separation problems, and that means in simple words that he can't be alone and he can't be together with somebody, both. So in a certain way, he's very dependent, and in the other way, he is very afraid of dependence, and that makes him walk in life as somebody walking on a string.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have just said to me brings to my mind another relationship. You spoke a great deal about manipulation. We could say that this is part of imagining things or representing things. Does representation and compensation, as a psychological defence mechanism, could that be related in this case, that is, representation, manipulation, and control on one side, and on the other side, compensation or possibly projection of a lack?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several types of defence mechanisms. You have the more primitive ones and the more higher ones. Every person has defence mechanisms, but in regard to Mr. Jelisic, you see especially the very primitive defence mechanisms, like, for example, denying or what we call splitting. Splitting means that you look at somebody in black/white terms. Somebody is completely good or completely bad and there is nothing in between. So that's something that Mr. Jelisic is doing quite often in the interview and also when he's talking about his life history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. We spoke a little bit about Mr. Jelisic's position, not as a victim but as perpetrator, as a criminal, if I could say it that way. In Mr. Jelisic's personality, is there also a victim side, even when he committed criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very interesting question, because as a psychiatrist, we look at the borderline personality disorder as a severe kind of disease, in fact, and if you have a disease, then you are certainly a victim. In my opinion, because of his emotional disturbances, he is, in a way, the victim of those disturbances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm almost at the end of my questions but I still have a few left. If we accept the fact that from a certain time of behaviour, one could see at least three steps in reaching it, that is, perception or knowledge, from the point of view of trying to get some information or to understand reality, that is, knowledge, and then the emotion which some people call emotional areas -- you spoke a great deal with emotional things -- and then after the final stage, which is action, if we were to put one next to the other, knowledge, emotions or emotionalism, and then action or behaviour, where would you see more problems? At what stage would you see more problems or more illness, in the concrete case, speaking about Mr. Jelisic's personality?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his emotional -- in his emotions, but his emotions will lead to behaviour. And a characteristic of his behaviour is impulsiveness. He is a little bit -- in Holland we have a saying, against the wall makes strange jumps. And he is a little bit like that. When he is put on the pressure, he can react very impulsively because he can't cope in a mature way with emotions, especially mixed emotions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I've understood you correctly, doctor, you didn't see any disturbances that were in relation to taking in information about reality, but more problems of analysing or seeing that reality? You didn't see illusions or delusions?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He has what we call psychotic symptoms. His capacity of seeing the reality is almost one hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question has to do with a question that Mr. Greaves asked you. To kill Muslims or to help Muslims, you said that that was somewhat contradictory, but I would like to ask you the following question: If we have an unstable personality; if we have an unstructured emotional personality, one which is not organised; if we have an individual who does not -- has not yet reached maturity, from the point of view of his personal identity; we end up with a person who is completely dependent on circumstances. And we have also seen that Mr. Jelisic's behaviour was especially manipulative and representative, if I can say that, if I can use theatrical terminology, that he was putting on a spectacle. Could we have a Mr. Jelisic in that type of personality who could kill Muslims, but at the same time could help Muslims under different circumstances, in practical terms, because theoretically it seems to me that there could be some contradictions. But you yourself said that one cannot make generalisations, but for the time being we are speaking about the personality of Mr. Jelisic. Could that happen?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can happen, yeah. That's a possibility. But it is a very difficult question to answer because it goes a little bit in what we call insanity defence, and therefore if you really want to ask this question, well, you need, as a psychiatrist, to have far more information. And you need more information about the circumstances during the crimes and, indeed, to have insight and witness accounts to make that picture complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are more familiar than I am with schizophrenia or in the emotional area where there is always a degree of emotional ambivalence. I think that in this case, in Mr. Jelisic's personality there is a confusion, an emotional confusion?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps he would be completely dependent on the circumstances in order to do what I have always called process of compensation. And as you said, in Mr. Jelisic's personality there is still a childish side. You know that frequently the child -- his behaviour is aimed at calling attention to it. So in light of that, could one still say that Mr. Jelisic behaves in a certain way in order to call attention to himself, in a way of -- showing that he obeys or he is obeying his superiors by killing people. But the same behaviour is used to call attention to himself when he helps Muslims in order to compensate for what he had done. That is another way of calling attention to himself. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you see it correct. That's right. The way you see it, he is looking for compensation in his behaviour and -- but he doesn't -- but that process is unconscious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. I agree with you. Yes, he does that. But not being fully conscious of it, but he does that. And I think that this is a process that can be used in order to understand the results, because we are now dealing with results.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: And specially he has problems with ambivalent feelings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have helped me understand a very difficult situation, to get into a human mind, but you have been very helpful to me, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Judge Riad would like to ask you another question. I myself have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. van den Bussche, this is really a continuation of a question which Judge Rodrigues has asked you. When he asked you if the accused would feel at the same time victimised, feel the victim while committing his acts, and your answer was -- generally you said that he is, after all, the victim of the disturbances of his character. Of course, this is -- of course he is the victim of himself. But then you mentioned the example of the cat, your Dutch proverb, I hope you will give it to us in Dutch. It's called a cat jumps when cornered, jumps when it is cornered. That was perhaps another answer. Does that mean that he, while committing these -- the crimes of which he is accused, he was, in fact, defending himself?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when you put Mr. Jelisic under big pressure, he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When you put --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Big pressure, big tension, and he is anxious, then he will react impulsively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: A big pressure. All right. Do you think that this, in this circumstance --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a stressful condition, when he is in a stressful condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You speak of anybody or of persons of this --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, about Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: About him?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If he is under great pressure?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Great pressure means that he is attacked?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, but it can also be verbal aggression, not physical aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So if one attacks him verbally?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Or would it be in his mind? If he feels that he is under great threat, he or his community, would that be a way of defence? Is that your answer to the question? Because the question was quite far reaching, that he is committing things as a way of defence. It's almost self-defence?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No. I am saying that he is a victim of his emotional disturbance and because we, as psychiatrists, see his personality disorder as a severe kind of disease, in fact, development disease. And most of those people have severe problems in normal life. They have problems with relations. They have problems with what we discussed before, the balance and autonomy. They most of the time have many partners or many jobs. They never finish a job, and they feel themselves empty inside. Some of them start to drink too much alcohol or go into drugs, and all those symptoms has Mr. Jelisic. And in only the last few years it looks like he, for the first time, has a more -- a little bit more mature relation with his wife, although his wife is very young. But I think that's the first normal relation 'til now he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But finally, all this -- to what extent does all this impair his discernment and his capacity to judge what he is doing, to know what he is doing?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knows what he is doing, but it influences his behaviour and his way of thinking about people. And also it leads to -- it influences his acting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But he knows the consequences of his acting?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knows the consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He is aware of it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spared you -- I am going to spare you a long series of questions. Otherwise, your voice is not going to hold out 'til the end. My colleagues asked you some very good questions that I myself would have liked to have asked. So mine will be relatively short. Obviously, if the questions are as detailed and as long as they are, it's because the procedure is set up in that way in this Tribunal. And it was the Defence's choice, we could not hear the accused, but that's how things are. And this is a choice of the Defence, which is a choice that the Defence can make, which explains why we have several questions to ask. In a way mediators in order to get into the personality of Mr. Jelisic. I will be very brief. I have a question in respect of Mr. Nice's relating to duress and remorse. Do you agree with me, or perhaps you don't agree with me, that one can have remorse, whether or not one has acted under duress?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You said that you could not answer the question as to whether he was still dangerous.
