utterances.text: Well, what I only looked -- I especially looked to what was related to our diagnostic examination, and that was the egocentric extent and his youth past in the former Yugoslavia. And what he does even more than in the diagnostic exam is that he feels no responsibility or guilt or whatsoever. Not about his -- I don't want to go into his statements about what he did in the war, but pre-war all his failures and deeds he did over there, or his fraud also, he relates that to other persons or other reasons and doesn't take responsibility for his deeds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question on remorse. Is there any evidence anywhere that this man has seen, in image or in description, the suffering of the people that he's killed, or indeed their loved ones and bereaved?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that. I think, as far as I can see, and I didn't examine the interviews on that point, but what he says in our diagnostic examination, and what I wrote about his examinations or the interviews, was that he cannot place himself in other -- in the shoes of somebody else. That's what I have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nice. We're going to try to finish now, with the agreement of my colleagues, so that we can release the witness. Let me turn to my colleagues immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] You just mentioned, in answer to the Defence counsel, that the qualitative psychiatric examination which was made was good, in answer to his question that apparently you did not have a full knowledge of the facts of the case. So still this examination would be qualitatively sufficient, if you do not know the facts of the case?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: It depends on the questioning we had to answer. The quality of a psychiatric examination has to do, first of all, with the questions you have to answer. Given the context, given the limited context we had, first of all, the fact that we had to do it in several days only, that we couldn't work it out like we do normally, come back again to the one we have to see and confront a person with dishonesty or other statements, or from people we interviewed also, given the limited context, I think we made a good report, especially for answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Now, Dr. van den Bussche, when I asked him, and you were present, about the relationship between the acts and between the personality disorder, he said that, in fact, the acts committed would have been more or less motivated by his personality disorder, were related to his personality disorder. Would you go as far as to say that he could not help committing these acts, his personality disorder put him under such a compulsion that these acts were bound to happen?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: It's a balance between circumstances and personality disorder. I think in a certain way they were bound to happen. I think the aspect which we did not talk about today, until now, maybe not enough, is his aspects of grandeur, his narcissistic aspects. He states in his examination, "Give a person a pistol and a Motorola and he thinks he is God." I think that that is a statement that he really felt grandeur, I think, and that aspect made it -- it's not only pressure and a cat against the wall, but also the grandeur, the narcissistic aspect. Another aspect of narcissistic problems is the rage which goes unread. So it's bound to happen, in a certain way, yes, in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speaking of the rage, I note that you mentioned his rage was close to the surface and his aggression was under the surface. What is the meaning of these terms, "close to the surface," "under the surface"?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: What we do in a psychiatric examination is -- in our training, we call that transference and countertransference. You use your feelings which the patient gives you as an instrument. We are trained for that. That was my answer also to Mr. Greaves. What you see -- what we saw and what we discussed as a team is that under slight confrontation or deviating the interview to topics we would like to discuss or to shortcut Mr. Jelisic's monologue, he became irritated. We kept it very polite, but there we felt, both of us, the anger, so we didn't want to confront him further. That's what I meant with "anger under the surface." And the narcissistic rage, that's a whole other item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Narcissistic rage, that's a whole other item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Which is also very quick to come.

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: No, in certain circumstances only, with extreme confrontation and in cat-against-the-wall situations, let's say, like that, if you're frustrated in your grandeur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not necessarily that you have to defend yourself; you are just proving your grandeur.

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Doctor. I have many questions, but I'll only ask some of them. You divided killers, murderers between homicides and other categories. I'm speaking in French and writing in English, so I'm mixing up the languages. What I would like to ask you is what is the sense of family that you're using here? Is it a restrictive sense or a broader sense? You know, we speak about a more nuclear family -- mother, father, children -- and an extended family. What sense are you using it in?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Close relationships.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can one include, in the notion of the extended family, one can see a certain feeling of belonging? Can one speak of an extended family if one is speaking about an ethnic belonging to --

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: [In French] Any belonging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was Jelisic's circumstances. The fact that he was a Serb and that he was part of that ethnic group doesn't play any role in that distinction?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: [In French] No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the question. You said that you were very surprised when you learned that Mr. Jelisic had lied about the question of torture by Croats. Why?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I wanted to respond in French. Because it's such a worked-out story, not only in our examination but also in the other things I read, and now that's all not true. So I was surprised by that because it's so worked-out, differentiated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if we take into account somebody, say an attorney, who asked them to tell that story, how would you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Well, then he learned his lesson well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the other aspect. You said, you said frequently in fact, the objective relations were somehow disturbed. I believe that you spoke about manipulation in that respect, that is, disturbances of his objective relations which was also the cause of the manipulation. This is my question: Is it possible that Mr. Jelisic manipulated people so that subsequently they could come to be defence witnesses for him?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: It might be -- it might be possible. I answer affirmative to that because certain topics we couldn't discuss with him. We couldn't discuss about how he got money for his kiosk, which was his friends, and I think there is a whole area we didn't touch on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only those areas that he wanted to touch on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I'm going to ask you a question, and then I'm going to tell you a story. Imagine that Mr. Jelisic were to come into a cafe, find a woman there, a woman who works in the cafe, and then after 20 minutes of conversation, Mr. Jelisic asks that woman to allow him to take her son, who I think at the time was four or five years old, to go spend a week's vacation with Mr. Jelisic, and the woman, that woman, that mother, allows him to do that. That was the first time that Mr. Jelisic saw the woman, the first time that the woman saw Mr. Jelisic. What comment do you have, from the point of view of manipulation, whose objective it was to have for himself defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: I think it's impressive -- sorry. Slower?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you answer, please.

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: I think it's impressive that a woman who talks 20 minutes to a man gives her child away for a week's holiday with a total stranger. For me, it's unimaginable. Two options arise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you. Imagine that that's true.

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Imagine? If the fact is there, then it's also impressive that Mr. Jelisic, in an amount of 20 minutes, can be so trustful for that lady to give her child to him for a week. That's very impressive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But from the perspective of what you knew about Mr. Jelisic's personality and that aspect of manipulation, would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: He comes very close in his relationships, yes, because he doesn't know the borders, he doesn't know the limits in the relationships.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. You said that Mr. Jelisic uses other people to satisfy his own needs. In some way, can killing satisfy someone with Mr. Jelisic's needs?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: I think I have to wait a bit here. We come to the issue of perversity, and maybe narcissistic rage also. It is possible, yes, that the anger, the rage he feels towards others, because they did him harm in his opinion, can reflect itself in doing harm to others. And if he has lust with it, we couldn't examine that because we didn't go for that issue, but it might be possible because Mr. Jelisic externalises and is angry at all those people who did wrong to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You spoke frequently about the egocentric nature, the narcissistic nature of Mr. Jelisic. Did you find any idea whether there were any references or ideas about paranoia, specifically in respect of the Serbs? Because he always said that he had to defend himself from the Serbs, that the Serbs were his worst enemies. Along with his egocentrism and narcissism, were there also some references made to paranoia in respect of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: What he said to us was -- I have to wait. What he said to us was that, in fact, he was a hero for the normal people and that he wasn't afraid of the people who were after him. I don't think that's true, the last issue. I think he said that out of his grandeur. If you're a great man, you're not afraid, but I cannot -- because we couldn't go into that issue because he didn't want to discuss it, I cannot comment further on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question I would like to ask you. You examined Mr. Jelisic in the presence of another person, so you had a degree of control over the manipulation. Did you also have some control over his body language, his non-verbal communication? That's my first question. If you say that you did, whether that body language was consistent with his verbal language.

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. That's part of our intervention, to do that. We normally discussed with each other the case, and we put our examination together, both of us. Body language was related to the issues he presented. That's why we can state that anger was under the surface. I mean, anger is not only -- transference and countertransference issues are related to body language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question. In order for you to conclude something about manipulation, do you look more at the emotions and feelings or do you look more at the knowledge itself or objective knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: I cannot say which one takes the lead. And it's matter of fact what we do, what we discuss now all the time is take issues out of traits of the personality disorder. But they interrelate to each other. If you talk about paranoid traits, it has to do with an objective relationship, it has to do with grandeur also, and that's how you come to a diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask the question a different way. Can there be manipulation even when one is telling the truth or part of the truth? And my last question is the following. I laughed a little bit with your colleague when he said that he -- that there is only one word to say snow, and I said that Eskimos had at least 20 words. This merely means that certain people have specialisations in certain areas, with a lot of words to see and to express reality. A very simple question. You can answer it if you like. As a specialist, as a psychiatrist, particularly a forensic psychiatrist, can you see more in two hours than an ordinary person in two years, or are we exaggerating somewhat?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Two hours and two years, there is a big difference. But I think, yes. In a certain way, yes. I am always impressed about -- and that's why I called it a super specialisation to Mr. Greaves. And it's in fact a super, super specialisation, because I am a forensic child and adolescent psychiatrist. And the expertise you have is related to making contacts, to avoid confrontation first, the facets of the interview, to go around difficult issues, et cetera, to see in body language, as he said before and in certain pronunciation of words or whatsoever what's up in people's minds. And I think, yes, expertise is a big -- enormous advantage. I am always impressed by people not seeing things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My really last question. You said that you didn't carry out any tests and that you needed to conduct other interviews, for instance, with his parents or with people who knew him in order to form certain opinions, because I think you always answered with a degree of precaution. You said, "I can go this far, but in order to go further I would need more instruments, more diagnostic instruments." What you said for sure, then, can be said with the amount of time that you had and with the instruments that you had available to you at that time; was that enough?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to ask you to be a little more patient, because through my colleagues questions they have spared me from having to ask you more questions. I am going to ask the interpreters for a little more patience. They have been here almost for an hour and three quarters. A very simple question. I am referring to your report which was prepared a year ago. You were asked to study three questions. Was there was a mental illness? And you said, no, that he had profound personality disorders, that he was a borderline personality. Then, would his mental state allow him to understand the nature of the accusations brought against him. You said yes, that he could reason, and that to some extent emotionally he would be able to understand those accusations brought against him. And the third question: Was he fit to appear? I consider the third question is really now outside of the scope of this trial. The second question is borderline, and the first we have already taken note of. So this is my question: Did you feel any kind of discomfort when you were called to testify here and to speak about a subject that you examined a year ago now?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: In a certain way, yes. But at the same time I tried to, like you stated before, in the context that we did our exams, to stay between the lines of what I can say. And so in a certain way discomfort, but I tried to manage the discomfort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you are satisfied with what you've done. That's fine. You have your own emotions and that's very reassuring. But I am rather surprised, doctor. Can a psychiatrist, a specialist, can he just make an abstraction of the development over the course of a year of a subject, about whom we are not going to say anything in terms of responsibility; who pleaded guilty; who for now two months -- well, even longer who has been in detention; who is very troubled, you saw that through the last psychiatric examinations; can a psychiatrist like yourself make an abstraction of any evolution over the course of -- and you who saw him a year ago, can you say now that he is this or that? He is going to develop this way or that way? Because in the end the Judges have not heard him at all, and you didn't speak to him except for a year ago, and it was only the other doctor that spoke to him more recently. But that's the only question I am going to ask because the other questions that needed to be asked were very well put by the Defence and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS
utterances.text: Between the limitations I already stated, yes. Like I said before, Dr. van den Bussche and I are working in the same office. Dr. van den Bussche discussed the matter with me not only to hear my opinions, which he already had on paper, or our opinions which he already had on paper, but to discuss his diagnostic assessment in a interview situation with us. And at the other end it must be said that, of course, Mr. Jelisic is unique. Of course there is fluctuation. But I made general statements about borderline personality disorder and possibilities of change. And in that context I made comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had said, in fact, that that was my last question. You can go back to your work. The Tribunal expresses its gratitude to the interpreters. Very well. We are going to resume the hearing in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have the interpreters rested? Fine. Insofar as possible, we are going to try -- if we can't, we can't -- but we're going to try to finish this evening so that tomorrow -- let me say this to Mr. Nice, perhaps he hasn't had his headset on but I know he speaks French very well -- I just wanted to say that insofar as possible, we're going to try to finish, insofar as possible, let the interpreters be reassured that it's that way so then tomorrow could be devoted to the final arguments. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Greaves has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I just want to deal with one matter whilst I think about it and while it's in relation to the evidence which has just been heard by the Tribunal. Your Honour will recall that I asked Dr. Duits about restrictions placed on him in relation to Dr. Petrovic. I wish formally to place it on the record that such a restriction was placed on the Defence, and we are not only prohibited from calling Dr. Petrovic but prohibited from making any reference at all directly to any diagnosis or treatment or statement that she had made about the defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm glad that you said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, then with the Chamber's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have nothing to say on that point. That's a matter entirely, I think, between the Defence and the Registry. The Chamber will recall that in relation to Dr. Duits, I sought the Chamber's leave to approach him and to ask him questions, he having been originally relied on by the Chamber, and I don't think there's any complaint to the fact that I have called him or relied on the passages of his evidence. I think it's a different issue entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, it was appropriate for you to raise that question. I think that we'll take this into account as part of the substantive questions. We'll move to the next witness, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, the last witness is one for whom statements in B/C/S and I think French have now been prepared and served, and it's entirely appropriate, given his much longer acquaintance with this case than mine, that Mr. Tochilovsky should take the last witness, and so he's going to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness asked for the same kind of protection as other witnesses, the pseudonym and facial image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness S, do you hear me? This is the Presiding Judge speaking to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. First, check to see that these are your names on the document that the usher is showing you. Show it to him. Show it to him. Don't hide it that way. Then you're going to take an oath. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may now be seated, Witness S. You have responded to the summons of the Prosecution to testify in the sentencing hearing in order to determine the penalty applicable to Goran Jelisic, the accused, who is to your left in this courtroom, who pleaded guilty to crimes against humanity, and only within that scope. Let me remind Mr. Tochilovsky that the witness has agreed, insofar as he is going to be a character witness in respect of Goran Jelisic, as you yourself said in your submissions. Having said this, I can tell you, Witness S, that you are being covered by very strict protective measures and that you can speak without any fear and in full serenity. Mr. Tochilovsky, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tochilovsky:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, you had an opportunity to read a summary of your statement, and is the summary correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spent some time in Luka camp in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when you were taken to the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: The 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I was taken to Luka by Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe Goran Jelisic's behaviour, his demeanour on that evening, that day when he took you to Luka and when you were in Luka? Can you describe his behaviour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, it was as if he had been drugged, to put it simply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he look like a person who was acting under order, who was reluctantly following any orders when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not receive any orders; he issued orders himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to have some examples of that, upon your arrival to the camp, did soldiers try to approach you immediately upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Goran Jelisic's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: He said, "Go away. Don't touch him. Do you want me to kill you like the others in the hangar?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by the investigator, you prepared a sketch of the Luka camp, of the place where you were kept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to put this sketch before the witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: This is a description of the office where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it the place where you were kept when you were in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Please, could you put your question more specifically. I did not understand it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the place where you were kept when you were at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes, temporarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any guards, soldiers, other camp personnel in that room as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, there were a few unknown persons, and there were about four or five persons in the room who were doing their own jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any orders given by Jelisic to those others present in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, to bring in a man from the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did soldiers follow his orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to his behaviour, how did he treat those detainees who were brought on his order to the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: His behaviour. Well, when he would bring them there into the office, this is the only way I can describe this, he would start interrogating them and then hitting them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: And then take them out and probably kill them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he took the second detainee out and then returned without him, did he tell you anything about how he treats those Muslim Croat detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. He said, "I do not rape. I do not mistreat. I only kill."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He say how many people he killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. He said, "This is my 83rd or 93rd from this morning."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic tell you what had happened to your friend Mevko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In short, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: First, he asked me whether I knew him and what he was to me. And I answered that I was a very good friend of his, since he did not have many friends and his family did not care about him very much. He said that he had killed the strongest man until then. He had fired two bursts of gunfire into him and in the morning he would go there, shoot him in the temple so that he'd finally be dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did Goran feel sorry about what happened to Mevko, that he killed Mevko? Did he express any remorse of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, he did not show any remorse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were leaving the camp with Jelisic, did Jelisic give any other orders to soldiers upon his departure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: When we were leaving the Luka camp, he ordered that this man, who said that a Serb was guaranteeing for him, should be killed before we would come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that all these orders he gave when you were in Luka were followed, that others followed his orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No. He carried out the orders himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he ordered to bring those people to take care of them, did those soldiers bring people, follow his orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Could you please put this a bit more specifically? I don't know what you are referring to exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness S, I know it's not very easy, but when you answer, if you would please turn toward the Judges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine, fine. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it isn't easy, but try to do that. Of course when the questions are asked, you listen to the person asking the questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Goran issued orders to those present in the room, to the soldiers to bring detainees to him. Did those soldiers follow his order, obey his orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a few questions on other detainees, actually some of them were witnesses, protected witnesses. So maybe we can go to private session to mention those names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, I'd like to ask you just a little bit, please, about how you come to be here in The Hague. When were you first approached with a view to giving evidence at The Hague? Can you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: About a month ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to know where you are living, but the place in which you are living at the present time, have you been living there for some time; if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I've been living there for a year and a half, in that particular place; for the time being I'm there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would there have been any difficulty of any kind in finding you, say, in March or April of this year in the area in which you live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Could you ask me that in more precise terms? I didn't follow you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this right: You weren't making a secret of where you were living; you were living openly in the community in which you live, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the case in March and April of this year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If somebody had wanted to come looking for you in that community, they would have had no difficulty in finding you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move, please, to the circumstances in which you were asked to make a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the case, that one or more investigators came to see you and conducted an interview with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before recording your statement, did any of those people tell you what it was they wanted to know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: If you would, please, be a little more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. The people who came to see you and to take a statement from you, did they, before they took a statement from you, tell you about what incident it was that they wanted to speak with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they describe to you the information which they had about that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No. I just gave them the information, because they asked for it, in connection with Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a question of them saying, "We want to know about an incident with Goran Jelisic on the 15th of May, 1992," or did they give you more information as to what it was they were seeking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: They just asked for that piece of information relating to the 15th of May, 1992, what happened there, and that was the kind of statement that I gave them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like just to put a bit of detail onto the account that you've given us this afternoon, Witness S. This is right, isn't it: that you say that you were working at a particular place during the course of the afternoon when Jelisic and another man came to see you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other man's name was Dzole. Is that the correct pronunciation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's correct, but I know that they mentioned that particular name during the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequently, you were taken from the place where you were working to the outside and put into a car; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the car, when you drove off from that place, were four people; is that right? Yourself, Goran Jelisic, Dzole, and another person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Four in all, including yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other person was a girl, a woman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I wouldn't say woman; I'd say girl. I thought she was probably about 14 or 15 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the house of the (redacted), had anybody else got into the car between the place where you were working and that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at the house, was the car parked close to the house and close to its entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. A car was parked close to the house, at the end of the road, by the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can just get it right, was the car within sight of the entrance of the house in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: From the entrance to the house?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes, you could see, but you would have to come out of the house because there were some steps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. How far from the entrance to the house and the steps was the car parked? Are we talking about five yards, ten yards, twenty yards? What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: About 10 to 13 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your position where you were in the car, were you able to see the entrance of the house clearly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Not very clearly. I couldn't see properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the entrance to the house, did anybody get out of the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic got out and went up to the front door of the house, and then he called the (redacted) and he went out after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, no other man had joined you at this time, had they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? I don't follow what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Whilst you were there at the house, no other person joined you. No other man, no other woman joined you, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I sat in the car, and next to the driver sat Monika. Goran Jelisic went out of the car and went over there, and later on, Dzole went out and took over (redacted). That was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Five people? Just a moment, please. Before that, we went towards the school, and when Goran Jelisic said, "Who's Dzodza?" I didn't understand him very well. When we got to the school, there were two people standing there. He also asked them who Dzodza was, and one of them said that he was (redacted) (redacted), and then he told them to drive him to the house. So perhaps you're thinking about those two individuals. Perhaps they were still there, but I did not notice them. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the people who were with you went eventually to the car belonging to (redacted); is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the others who were with you, apart from Goran and Dzole, get out of the car at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Only myself and Monika remained in the car after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dzole go in towards the house after Goran and (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so because I didn't see it. So I can't really say; I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to get back to Brcko, two cars were taken there, is that right, one of which was the car belonging to (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just describe to us the seating arrangements in the two different cars. Who went in which car, Witness S?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: As far as I know, Dzole was in (redacted) car, that is to say (redacted), and in the other car there was Goran Jelisic, Monika and myself. And later on we were joined by another soldier whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were joined in your car or, sorry, not your car, but the car in which you were seating by another soldier whose name was never given to you; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the only person who was in the car with (redacted) was this man whose name was Dzole? No question of there being anybody called Simo with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I was quite lost at the time, to tell you frankly, so possibly there was, but not really. There are two versions. I can't say that it's the truth or whether it's the truth, because I was very frightened at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You travelled to Brcko. The other car only contained (redacted) and one other person; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that's right, because they went off before us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Monika remained with you in your car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Luka, you were taken to the office and (redacted) was already there. That's right according to your statement; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if (redacted) said that you were already there at the time, not the other way around, that wouldn't be right, would it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It's very probable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people in all were in the office when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember those details. I know that (redacted) was there and probably another man next to him. All I know is that I tried to sit down there and at that time they took my handcuffs off. He took the handcuffs off my right hand so that I was able to sit down. But how many people were there, I can't really say because I don't really -- didn't really notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there was some difficulty in getting the handcuffs off, but you managed to get them off after a short while; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that simply a problem of somebody not being able to get the key in properly and to get the handcuff off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I don't know, but they couldn't find the right key to the handcuffs. So that they tried to pry them open with a pin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And eventually they managed to get them off all right, did they, without any further fuss?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes. From one hand. And after some time they got them off the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, according to you, and I'll come back to this in a little while, Witness S, instructions were given to go and fetch one person, who was brought back, a detainee who was brought into the office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And between your arrival in the office and instructions being given to fetch that detainee, was any interrogation conducted of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I had my head bowed down all the time and I was extremely frightened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your account is this: That three detainees were brought into the office and taken out again, one after another. It wasn't a question of three detainees being brought in at once, was it, according to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular detail. All I know is that they would take one by one in. Whether they were all three in there together, I really can't say. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if Witness R said after a short while he brought in three young men between 20 and 25, that wouldn't be right either, would it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll read to you a short piece of evidence. It's said: Q What did he do with that man? What did he ask of that man? A He said bring those people in. Q What happened to the list with the names on it?" And he then described the particular individual taking a folder. And then this: "After a short while he brought in three young men between 20 and 25 years of age." A clear implication of that being that three people were brought in at once. That can't be right, if you are telling the truth, Witness S, can it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is right? You said, "That is right." I didn't understand this answer. That's right that you are not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember. As far as I remember, and as far as I know, they were brought in one by one, one by one prisoner was brought in. I don't remember that they brought in three at the same time. Perhaps I am wrong, but that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, when you made your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, it was read over to you in the Bosnian language, wasn't it, at the end of making it? Do you remember that? And we are talking about just four or five days ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told them and signed that it was -- the statement was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this. What statement are you referring to? In relation to what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other statements have you made in relation to this incident, Witness S? A written statement reduced into writing and read over to you, how many other statements have you made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Written statements? I don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder whether he might see the original of the work which has been provided to the Defence, please. Just so we know exactly what we are talking about. Would you be so kind, Witness S, as to look at that document, please. Don't read it yet. You see at the bottom of the first page of that document a signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the bottom of each of the following pages. Do those bear your initials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And don't look at the last page, but look at the last but one page, please, Witness S. Do you see there -- I think you've got the English version, I hope. A short piece of text at the top and then a box with some words in it, and again your signature on there. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember signing those pages and initialling those pages on the 17th of November 1999 -- sorry, seven days ago. I do apologise. I mislead you as to time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the statement which you made and which was reduced into writing, the statement you made to the Office of the Prosecutor, Witness S?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you accept that it was read over to you in the Bosnian language, at the end of which you signed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you need to have a Bosnian version put in front of you, because I am quite happy that you should have it so you can follow what I am saying. Would that help you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then please may he have the Bosnian version. Again, if -- I would just like you to look at the page we were just looking at, which I think will be the last but one. And it's the end of that page where it says, I think in your language, "witness acknowledgment." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that witness acknowledgment reads as follows, doesn't it, "This statement has been read over to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you accept from me that in the statement that you made, as indeed you told us this afternoon, that the detainees were brought in one by one, and not three at a time? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I accept, to the best of my recollection, but I do not preclude the possibility of this not being correct because I was very upset at the time. I was not exactly composed. I had seen and heard quite a few things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, the point is this, that the two accounts which you've been given about this incident are in material respects completely different. And the differences which I pointed out to you mean that they cannot both be true. That's right, isn't it, Witness S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't give the witness an answer. The problem with differences under such dreadful circumstances has already been pointed out before to the Court. You are not dealing with scientific experts, what you are discussing. This is May 1992 in a hangar, which is simply hellish. So you can simply point out things, but don't try to give the witness an answer. If you agree, perhaps you might try to move a little bit more quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The account of the alleged Russian roulette that you give. Is this right? You said to the Office of the Prosecutor that the gun was pointed at the head or temple of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, that's what I assume. The head, for instance, because he was sitting next to me, and the pistol was right next to me, like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were right close to it at that point; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no question of it being pointed at the chest of (redacted) and the trigger pulled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Well, it is very possible, but I imagine somewhere in the head. That's what I assumed, judging by the level at which the pistol was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were removed from Luka and taken back to where you had come from, how many checkpoints in all did you pass through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I'll give you an approximate number. Perhaps five checkpoints where we did not stop; we stopped only at the first and second one on our way back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the way home, only two checkpoints did you stop at.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No. I said perhaps about five, but we were only stopped at the first and second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the question that I asked you. As far as you could see, the incidents involving these three detainees which you claim to have witnessed, you cannot say, can you, if, prior to your arrival, any orders were given in relation to those detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: I could not have seen that or heard that because I was not there, nor do I know of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that it's quite clear, and I'll put it quite shortly to you, Witness S, there were no killings that afternoon; there was, I suggest, no game of Russian roulette and no ill-treatment of any person in your presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is your opinion, Mr. Greaves, and you can argue that tomorrow. Ask questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to him that if he's saying there were such incidents, that it's not true. He's entitled to have an opportunity to deal with that proposition, and I put it to him so that he may deal with the proposition that it's not true. That is a proper issue which goes to the question of credit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Challenging the question itself, the credibility of your question. You have a right to ask questions, but I'm simply contesting the way you ask questions. Not by saying "I suggest that" but by saying that you were making assertions. Move to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I've made it plain what our position is. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Tochilovsky. Re-examined by Mr. Tochilovsky:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question in regard to those answers you gave to the Defence about those three detainees who were brought to the room. Do you know what happened to those detainees after they were beaten, as you described, by Goran and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: This is the way I'm going to put it: The first one was taken outside. I heard two blunt shots. I could not see that. I did not see that because I could not see that. You could not really see this with your own eyes through that hall. The second one, he took out, and I heard three blunt shots, and after the second one, his trousers had blood stains on them. The third one was returned to the hangar and the fourth one was taken out to wait.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That one is the one who Goran, upon his departure, ordered to kill as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: No. That one was already at the hangar. The fourth one who was waiting there was a distant relative of mine. Until the present day, I don't know what's happened to him. At that point, while I was there, he was still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Goran took those people out and you heard those shots, did he look like a person who was acting under any order, or was feeling any remorse for or sorry for what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: First of all, as far as I could tell, he was totally in charge over there. As for remorse, I did not see anything like that in his face. All of this was in cold blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tochilovsky. Judge Riad? Judge Rodrigues? I have a very short question to ask you. When Goran took the pistol in that dreadful Russian roulette game, was the gun loaded? Were there a certain amount of bullets? Was there one bullet or were there several bullets? If you remember. Perhaps you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: It was loaded because I know that he was taking bullets out, and how many he returned, that, I don't know. Basically, I didn't even want to see it because the very words, "Russian roulette," made me realise that my life was threatened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I'm not really interested in knowing how many there were. I just simply wanted to know whether the gun was really loaded with some bullets, either one or several.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Several.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, I wouldn't be wrong when I say that Goran Jelisic took a real risk when he put the gun to his temple.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS S
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. That's all. It was a bit difficult for you, but thank you for having come. I hope --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you're going to go home at peace and try and forget all of that, if it's possible. You will be taken care of, and once again, my colleagues and I would like to thank you. I know it's difficult. You have the right to have a good beer when you get out of here, if you like beer, a Dutch beer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just add one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came here and I was welcomed very nicely, but there is just one regret I have: I'm so sorry that this trial cannot last longer because there are so many things to be said. That's all I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that the International Tribunal hears somebody saying that the trials should be even longer than they are. Thank you very much. We are going to adjourn until tomorrow morning at 10.00, I believe it is; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean you hope so?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because there is a further initial appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, yes. Judge Rodrigues spoke to me about that. Mr. Greaves, did you want to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: At whatever moment is convenient to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply wanted to ask a question. Mr. Nice or Mr. Tochilovsky, about how long will your final arguments take? About how long? I'm trying to organise the Trial Chamber's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should hope I could be done in two hours. I've reduced the arguments to paper, which will be ready tomorrow, and so I will be able to pass over various paragraphs, and I have a schedule of evidence that, again, I can pass over quickly. I hope two hours, not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And you, Mr. Greaves, about how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have no idea at the moment because I shall be working all night completing it, and I don't know at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that we'll be able to finish by the end of tomorrow. That's what I would hope for. Since you do need to go to sleep, I'd ask that you not work all night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two matters that I want to raise, please. Your Honour directed that a report should be obtained from the commandant of the detention unit. I have not yet had sight of such a report and I would inquire whether such a report has been received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, did you get that report?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't have it. I could see after the hearing where things stand, but I think that ordinarily the report should be ready. I was thinking that it would be ready by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I didn't know of the deadline and I had become anxious about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you're right. You're absolutely right, Mr. Greaves. In any case, we have to be finished by tomorrow evening at the latest. We would ask the registrar to be sure that Mr. Greaves has the report, and the Judges also. The Judges can think about it afterwards, but Mr. Greaves has to present his final arguments tomorrow. Second point, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have presented a number of documents to my learned friend, and he has been cogitating carefully about them, but we're getting to the stage where he really does need to make up his mind as to whether he's going to allow me to present them to Your Honours without any further argument. I think they're relatively non-controversial as documents go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy to allow them to go in, providing that there is another document that my learned friend, which I haven't yet shown him, I think, is prepared to go in. It's to do with medical records and service records and matters of that sort. If I can just show him this document tonight, I dare say we can agree that the whole package can go in tomorrow morning, and we'll have this document copied in enough numbers for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I thank my learned friend for his remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I want to thank the interpreters. We will adjourn and we should begin at 10.00 tomorrow. Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 6.13 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of November, 1999, at 10 a.m. 22 23 24 25
